t: Reading the machine while it runs
html:
Programming is mostly watching. Logix Connect gives you several windows onto a running controller, and each answers a different question.

  • The ladder, online. True instructions light green; a timer shows its accumulator counting; a rung that should be true and is not shows you which instruction breaks the path. This is where you start.
  • Controller Tags → Monitor Tags: every tag, live. Expand a DINT to see its bits; open a TIMER to see .ACC and .DN. Click a BOOL value (or Ctrl+T on its row) to toggle it while testing; the toolbar’s Toggle button toggles the bit selected in the ladder.
  • Quick Watch (View → Quick Watch, Alt+3): your own short list of tags with live values, floating or docked at the bottom.
  • The I/O Monitor: the chassis, point by point, with the device and signal wired to each point and the rungs that use it. When a sensor “does not work”, this is where you find that it is wired to a point your rung does not read.
  • Trends (Window → New Trend…, or right-click any tag → Trend): up to eight pens on a strip chart, sampled as often as every scan. The tank level falling with every charge and rising when the inlet opens is a thing you have to see once.
  • The Simulator Log: what the machine did, in its own words. Each line is a bug report with the device’s name in it: a capper that cycled with no bottle under it, a bottle pushed off by a gate with nothing to land on, a shredder that ground with no box under it.

Cross Reference (Ctrl+E, or right-click an operand) lists every instruction that uses a tag, in every routine: the rung, the exact reference (T1.DN, T1.ACC) and a Y under Destructive where the instruction writes it. An alias and the address it points at are found together. Find (Ctrl+F) searches rung text and comments.

I/O forcing works as on a real controller: in Monitor Tags click the Force Mask cell of an I/O point (or of a tag aliased to one) to force it on, off or to a value, and the forces take effect while Communications → I/O Forcing: Enable All is on. That is how you test an output rung before the sensor that drives it is fitted. Tools → Clear Tag Values zeroes timers, counters and bits without touching the machine; Reset Sim does the machine as well.

In the app

Tools → Inject Machine Fault… breaks something on the machine (a jammed gate, a sensor that sticks, an overload) so you can practise finding it with these windows, and Tools → Fault Drill… does it as a timed exercise. Part IV’s step 11 writes the alarms that catch them.
